hook: From the long summer roads of nineteen fourteen to the silence at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of nineteen eighteen, the four years of the Western Front, told softly, so you can rest.
narration:
Tonight we travel to the Western Front of the Great War. Speak softly. Let the lamp grow dim. Slow your breathing. We will walk together from the warm meadows of August nineteen fourteen, through four winters of mud and snow, to the still morning when the guns finally fall silent. There is no urgency in this journey. The years will pass at their own pace. Lean back, close your eyes if you like, and let the long summer of Europe begin again.

In the early days of August nineteen fourteen, the harvest is still standing in the fields between the Meuse and the Moselle. Children chase each other along village lanes. Old men sit on benches in the small town squares of Lorraine and Champagne, and in the orchards of Belgium the apples are coming on. Then, almost without warning, columns of grey-uniformed soldiers begin to move west along dusty roads. The German Empire has set in motion the largest mobilization Europe has ever seen. Millions of men leave their homes, board trains, and travel in long, patient lines toward the frontier.

The German plan has been written years before, by a chief of staff named Schlieffen. He has imagined a great wheel, swinging through the low countries, sweeping past Paris from the north, and crushing the French armies against the eastern fortresses. By the summer of nineteen fourteen, Schlieffen is dead, and his successor, a thoughtful, careful man named Moltke the Younger, has revised the plan and softened its right wing. Still, the principle remains. To win in the west, the German army must move quickly, march far, and fight without rest.

On the fourth of August, German troops cross the border into neutral Belgium. The Belgian army is small, but the country is full of forts. The first obstacle is the ring of concrete and steel around the city of Liège. Belgian gunners fire from beneath thick domes of armored cement. German engineers bring up their largest siege guns, the great howitzers known as Big Berthas, and one by one the forts collapse under their slow, deliberate fire. The road is open. German cavalry trots westward, lances upright, into a country that did not expect war.

Across the channel, the British government meets late into the night. By the morning of the fifth of August, Britain has declared war as well, in defense of Belgian neutrality. Within days, the small, professional British Expeditionary Force begins to land at French ports. They are a long-service army, well drilled in rifle fire, and they will soon meet the advancing German columns at a coalfield town called Mons.

On the morning of the twenty-third of August, along a sleepy canal in southern Belgium, the British infantry fire their first volleys of the war. Their rifle drill is so rapid that the German troops in front of them believe they are facing massed machine guns. The British line holds for a day, then must give ground, because to the south the French have failed in their own offensive in Lorraine, and the entire Allied front is being pressed backward. So begins the great retreat. For two weeks, the British and French armies fall back across northern France, marching by night, sleeping in fields, eating what they can, while the heat of late summer presses down on them. The roads fill with refugees. Carts laden with mattresses and bird cages. Old women in shawls leading goats by frayed ropes. Soldiers and civilians moving south together, quietly, almost dazed.

In Paris, the government prepares to leave for Bordeaux. The city seems on the edge of falling. But to the east, the French commander-in-chief, a stout, calm general named Joffre, is gathering his forces for a counterstroke. He sees an opening as the German wheel begins to drift inward, missing Paris on the wrong side, exposing its flank along a quiet river called the Marne. On the sixth of September, Joffre gives a simple order to all his armies: advance, attack, hold their ground. The French and British turn around together and begin to push back.

The military governor of Paris, an old colonial soldier named Gallieni, sees that he can speed reinforcements to the new front by sending six thousand soldiers in the city's red Renault taxicabs. The taxis trundle out of Paris into the September dusk, headlights flickering, dust rising behind them. They become one of the small, beloved images of the war. For five days the Battle of the Marne grinds on, until at last the German armies, exhausted, far from their railheads, low on shells, give up the great wheel and pull back to the heights above the river Aisne. There they begin to dig.

What happens next will set the shape of the war. Each side tries to outflank the other to the north, and each time their flanks meet first, in a long, exhausted handshake of trenches. The line stretches toward the channel coast, through Picardy, through Artois, through Flanders. By the autumn rains, the trenches reach the sea near Nieuport. There is no flank to turn. The war has run out of room to move.

In late October and through November, the Germans make one final attempt to break through, in the Belgian town of Ypres. The fighting in the muddy fields and shattered woods around Ypres is desperate. The British regulars who fight there suffer terribly. By the time the rains turn the ground to a thick, gripping clay and the snow begins, that small, professional army of August has nearly bled away, and a new army of volunteers is being raised at home in its place. The line holds. And so the year nineteen fourteen ends with the soldiers settled into their first winter trenches, lighting small fires of charcoal in tin pots, sharing tobacco, learning the names of the men beside them.

The retreat from the German wheel does not stop at the river Aisne. Through the long, bright weeks of late September and early October, the two sides reach for each other to the north, looking for any open flank. Columns of men march at the wide pace through the rolling country of Picardy and Artois, racing for the ground beyond. Each evening, fresh trenches are scratched into the chalk. Each morning, machine guns begin to fire across the gap. The line slowly lengthens. By the middle of October, it has reached the lowlands of Belgium, and then the canals and dykes of the river Yser. There, the small Belgian army, still under its King Albert, holds a thin sector along the coast. When the German pressure becomes too heavy, Belgian engineers open the sluices and let the cold North Sea pour back into the polders. The fields become a shallow inland sea, silver under the autumn moon. Behind that flooded country, the line at last has its anchor. There is no more flanking to be done.

In the small Belgian town of Ypres, the British and the French take the southern half of the new salient. The town itself is a place of Gothic spires and narrow medieval streets, and the great cloth hall in its centre has stood for seven hundred years. For nearly a month, from late October into November, the German army hammers at the salient. The Prussian Guard advances through the rain-soaked hop fields. They are met with disciplined rifle fire from old British regiments, the Coldstream and the Black Watch, the Worcesters, the Sherwood Foresters, who hold their thin lines through one bad day after another. There are moments when only a handful of cooks and drivers and signallers stand between a German breakthrough and the open road to Calais, and in those moments, somehow, the line holds. By the time the first heavy snows fall over the salient in mid-November, the regular British army that crossed to France in August is largely gone. New men, drawn from the volunteer divisions raised at home, will take their place.

The French armies further south have suffered no less. In Lorraine and the Vosges, in the Argonne forest, on the heights above the Aisne, regiments that had marched out of barracks in the warm August nights now stand in cold, sodden trenches, in greatcoats stiff with mud. France has lost more than three hundred thousand men killed in the first five months of fighting alone, and many more wounded. In Berlin, in Paris, in London, the casualty lists begin to be printed in the newspapers, in long, fine columns of small type, day after day. People learn to scan first for their own names, and then for the names of streets and villages they know.

On Christmas Eve, in some places along the line, the singing begins. Soldiers raise small candles on the parapets. German voices can be heard singing the carol Stille Nacht. British voices answer with Silent Night. In the morning, in scattered places between Armentières and the Yser, a few brave souls climb out of their trenches without weapons and meet in the no-man's-land between, and exchange small gifts and photographs and shake hands. It does not happen everywhere, and where it happens, the staffs of both sides quickly forbid it. But it happens. For one short morning, in the cold mist between the wires, the soldiers see each other simply as men.

With the new year, the trench line hardens. What had been improvised ditches becomes a permanent geography. Two parallel scars, a few hundred yards apart, run for some four hundred and fifty miles, from the dunes of the North Sea to the wooded hills of the Vosges, where the line meets the neutral border of Switzerland. Behind each front trench is a support trench, and behind that a reserve trench. Communication trenches connect them, narrow and zig-zagged so that a shell bursting in one section will not blast straight along the others. Sandbags rise on the parapet. Wooden duckboards lie on the floor. Beyond the front trench, a belt of barbed wire, sometimes thin, sometimes a hundred yards deep, stretches into the open ground.

Life in this geography settles into a grim routine. Before dawn, every man stands to arms, watching for an attack from the mist. After full daylight, the cooks bring up tea and bacon. Snipers scan for movement. By day, men sleep when they can, in dugouts hollowed into the trench wall, lined with whatever boards and tarpaulins they can find. After dark, ration parties carry food and water and ammunition forward along the communication trenches, often slipping in the mud. Wiring parties go out into no-man's-land to repair the belts of barbed wire. Patrols crawl along listening posts in shell holes. Most nights, somewhere along the long front, a flare goes up, and machine guns chatter for a moment, and then there is silence again.

The ground itself becomes an enemy. Rain fills the trench bottoms with cold, clinging water. Men's feet swell and crack from constant wet, a condition the doctors call trench foot. Lice live in the seams of every uniform, and no amount of boiling can defeat them. Rats grow fat on the bodies in no-man's-land and the spilled rations of the line. The smell of the trenches becomes its own permanent thing, a mixture of cordite, chloride of lime, wet wool, and the faint, sweet undertone of decay.

The armies look for ways to break this stalemate. In April nineteen fifteen, near the Belgian town of Ypres, the Germans try a new weapon. On the afternoon of the twenty-second, French colonial troops from Algeria and Morocco see a strange green-yellow cloud rolling toward them along the ground. It is chlorine gas, released from cylinders in the German front line. Men begin to cough and choke. Some run. Some fall and do not rise. The German infantry follows behind the cloud, but they too are uncertain of what they have done, and the gap they make in the Allied line is closed before they can fully exploit it. Canadian troops, holding the next sector, fight on with handkerchiefs soaked in water and urine pressed against their faces, the only protection they have.

Within days, both sides are racing to develop gas masks. Within months, both sides are firing gas of their own, in shells, in mortar bombs, in great projector batteries. There will be chlorine, and phosgene, and later mustard gas, which sears the lungs and blisters the skin. Gas does not break the trenches. It simply adds another layer of fear to the ones already there.

While the soldiers in the trenches dig deeper, a strange new battlefield is opening above them. The aeroplane is barely ten years old in nineteen fifteen, and yet pilots in canvas-and-wire machines are climbing into the sky to look down at the enemy positions. At first they only observe. They drop notes in weighted bags. They take photographs from leather-cased cameras. Then they begin to carry pistols, and rifles, and small bombs to drop by hand. Then they mount machine guns, and fire across the gap of air, until one Dutch designer named Fokker, working for the Germans, finds a way to fire a machine gun forward, through the propeller arc, by synchronizing the gun with the spinning blades. For a few months in late nineteen fifteen and early nineteen sixteen, this small invention gives the Germans the upper hand in the sky over the front. Pilots like Oswald Boelcke and Max Immelmann make the first names known in the new craft of the dogfight. The era of the lone air ace begins.

The ground war remains heavy and slow. Through the year nineteen fifteen, the French make great offensives in Champagne and Artois. The British try to break through at Neuve Chapelle, at Aubers Ridge, at Loos. Each time, the result is the same. A few hundred yards of broken ground are taken at the cost of tens of thousands of casualties, and a few weeks later the position settles back into its old shape. By the end of the year, the war on the Western Front has become a thing without an obvious end.

In the spring of nineteen fifteen, the British make their first carefully prepared attack of the new war, in the village of Neuve Chapelle. For the first time, the artillery fires a brief, intense bombardment instead of the long, slow shelling of nineteen fourteen. The infantry break into the German line on the first morning. But the reserves are slow, the telephones cut, the orders late. Within three days, the gain is fixed at a few hundred yards. The pattern that will haunt the Western Front for two more years, of a brilliant first hour and a stalled second day, is being written.

In May, in the soft hills of Artois, the French throw themselves at the high ground above Vimy ridge and Souchez. Joffre's plan calls for a great breakthrough. The reality is fields of unburied dead and a few yards taken at the price of whole regiments. In September, the British and French try again together, on a wider front, at Loos and in Champagne. At Loos, the British use chlorine gas of their own for the first time. The wind shifts, and some of it drifts back over their own trenches. The new volunteer divisions, the first to be made up entirely of Kitchener's men, the office workers and shop clerks who answered the great recruiting posters of nineteen fourteen, fight their first battle. They take the German front line. They are then thrown forward into a second German line that none of the staff officers had quite expected to find still intact, and there they fall in their tens of thousands.

Meanwhile, behind the lines, both sides are racing to industrialise the war. Munitions factories spring up on the outskirts of London, of Birmingham, of Lyon, of Essen. Whole villages of red brick rise around them, full of women, the wives and sisters and daughters of the men in the trenches, who turn shells on great lathes through twelve-hour shifts. Their faces and hands stain yellow from the trinitrotoluene in the explosives, and they earn the nickname canaries. In Berlin, the Hindenburg programme begins to mobilize the entire economy of Germany toward the production of guns and shells. In Britain, a young politician named Lloyd George becomes Minister of Munitions, and through that office begins to make himself the master of the British war effort. The line on the map barely moves, but the countries behind it are being reshaped almost beyond recognition.

Further south, the war spreads. In May, Italy joins the Allies and opens a new front against Austria-Hungary in the high stone country of the Isonzo river and the Dolomites. In the Balkans, Serbia, after holding off two Austrian offensives, is overrun in the autumn by a combined German, Austrian, and Bulgarian attack. The remnants of the Serbian army make a long, terrible winter retreat across the mountains of Albania, to be picked up at last by Allied ships at the Adriatic coast. On the eastern front, the great Central Powers offensive of nineteen fifteen drives the Russian armies back hundreds of miles, all the way to the swamps of the Pripet. But Russia does not surrender. The trains keep running. New armies are raised. The war goes on.

In the air over the Western Front, the slow accumulation of skill begins. A young German pilot named Boelcke writes the first set of rules for air combat, the dicta that pilots will study for two more decades. He pairs with another quiet, methodical young man named Manfred von Richthofen, the son of a minor noble from Silesia. The British and the French build their own air services. Pilots take off in the cold dawn, sometimes only fifty hours of training behind them, and look down at the brown ribbon of trenches, and at the small figures crawling along it, and try to fix their positions in their notebooks.

In the dim light of January nineteen sixteen, a German general named Falkenhayn, the chief of the great general staff, sits down with his maps and reaches a quiet, terrible conclusion. The Western Front cannot be broken in any usual sense, he believes. Trenches are too deep, machine guns too thick. So he proposes another idea. He will choose a single point on the French line, a place the French cannot afford to lose for reasons of pride and national feeling, and he will force them to feed every reserve they have into its defense. He will, in his own phrase, bleed France white. The point he chooses is an old fortified city on the river Meuse, with a ring of nineteenth century forts on the hills above it. Its name is Verdun.

Verdun stands on a salient, a bulge in the line where the front juts eastward. It is reachable from German territory by a thick web of railway lines. The French, by contrast, can supply it only along a single secondary road that runs north from a small town called Bar-le-Duc. Falkenhayn assembles a great mass of artillery, more than fourteen hundred guns, in a small, narrow front. On the morning of the twenty-first of February nineteen sixteen, after a day delayed by snow, his guns begin to fire.

The bombardment lasts nine hours. To the soldiers in the front trenches, it does not feel like an attack so much as the end of the world. Trees are stripped of branches. Bunkers collapse. Whole companies vanish. When the German infantry advance, they find the front line shattered, and they take it quickly. Within four days, they have captured the great fort of Douaumont, on the high ground above the city, almost without a fight. The French commander on the spot is a calm, lean general named Pétain, who is summoned in haste from his rest billet. He arrives at Verdun in the snow, ill with a chest infection, and immediately sets to organizing the defense.

His insistence is simple. The forts and ridges around Verdun must be held, but no division must be left in the line so long that it breaks. He institutes a system of constant rotation, sending each division forward for a brief, terrible week or two, then pulling it back to rest. Almost the entire French army will pass through Verdun before the year is out. To feed this rotation, he organizes the single road from Bar-le-Duc into a continuous, day-and-night stream of trucks. At its peak, a vehicle passes a given point every fourteen seconds, a great river of supply rolling north through the dust and snow. The French call this road the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, and the name fits.

The battle becomes a slow, grinding contest of artillery and small attacks. The German army inches forward. They take Mort-Homme, the Dead Man's Hill, and then the bare slopes of Côte trois cent quatre, Hill three hundred and four, where men lie unburied for weeks because no one can cross the ground to reach them. The French give ground, then take it back, then give it again. Pétain is moved to a higher command, and a more aggressive general named Nivelle takes over the active defense. Under him, a fierce subordinate named Mangin begins a series of counterattacks. In October nineteen sixteen, Mangin's men retake Fort Douaumont in a single, beautifully prepared assault. In December, they take Fort Vaux back as well. The German tide that had carried them within sight of Verdun's spires recedes.

When the battle is finally allowed to die away in the cold of late nineteen sixteen, more than three hundred thousand French and German soldiers are dead, and many more are wounded. Falkenhayn has been removed from his post months earlier. France has not been bled white, but it has been wounded in a way that will mark it for a generation. Pétain has become a national figure. The hills above the Meuse are stripped of life. To this day, in the woods around Verdun, the ground is still cratered, and the soil is still threaded with the iron of forgotten shells.

The defenders of Verdun build their daily life around the rotation. A division comes up by night, marching in column along the Voie Sacrée, the men silent in the cold, the trucks groaning past them in low gear. They reach the support trenches and shelter in dugouts cut into the limestone. After a short rest, they go forward into the front line, into shell holes that have been emptied of their previous tenants only hours before. They hold for a week, sometimes for two. They are pushed back, or they push forward a few yards, or they simply endure. Then, in the dark, another column comes up to relieve them, and they file back along the same road, hollow-eyed, gun-deaf, smelling of cordite and damp wool. Almost three quarters of the entire French army will pass through Verdun in the course of nineteen sixteen. Many will return more than once.

For the German soldiers, the experience is no less heavy. They too are brought up by trains and roads, but their salient at Verdun is narrower, and their losses to French counter-batteries on the open slopes are constant. Whole regiments of Bavarians, of Saxons, of Württembergers, are bled in the long climb up to Mort-Homme and Hill three hundred and four. The Crown Prince, the eldest son of the Kaiser, holds nominal command of the German Fifth Army on this front. Soldiers in his ranks come to call him, behind their hands, the Butcher of Verdun, though the orders that drive them forward come from far higher up.

Far to the east, while Verdun grinds on, the Russian army makes a great effort of its own. In June, an able and modest general named Brusilov attacks the Austro-Hungarian line in Galicia. He uses many of the same ideas the Western armies are slowly learning. Short, intense bombardments. Many small breakthroughs at once. Reserves close behind the assault waves. His armies advance more than fifty miles in places, take some four hundred thousand prisoners, and bring Austria-Hungary to the edge of collapse. Germany has to send divisions east, away from Verdun and from the new front being prepared on the river Somme. The pressure on the Western Front eases, just a little, for the first time in months.

At the same time, far out at sea, the navies of Britain and Germany clash for the only time in great strength, in the misty grey water off the coast of Jutland. For an afternoon and a long, confused night in late May, dreadnoughts and battlecruisers fire at one another at extreme range. The British lose more ships, but the German fleet does not break the British blockade, and after that battle the great German warships return to harbour and stay there for the rest of the war. The hunger blockade, the slow, patient choking of the German economy by Allied warships, will continue, year after year, into the kitchens and the ration queues of the cities of central Europe.

In the November of nineteen sixteen, when the first heavy snow at last allows the staffs to call the battle of Verdun ended, the slopes around the city are stripped of every tree, every blade of grass. Whole villages near the line, places like Fleury and Douaumont, are gone. They have been shelled until there is nothing left to mark where they stood, except a mound of broken brick and a sign post pushed into it, naming the village whose ground this used to be. After the war, those villages will be left as they are, fields of memorial silence, where a small chapel stands in the empty grass and where, by official order, no one has ever rebuilt a single house. The dead of both sides, gathered slowly through the rest of the war and the years after, will lie at last under a single great ossuary, a long, low stone hall on the ridge above the river. Through small windows in its walls, on certain afternoons, you can still see the bones inside.

While Verdun is grinding through its bitter spring and summer, far to the northwest, on a chalky, gentle landscape in northern France, another offensive is being prepared. The British high command, under a careful Scottish general named Haig, has agreed to attack on the river Somme, partly to ease the pressure on the French at Verdun, and partly because this is where the new British armies, the volunteer divisions raised by the great recruiting campaign of nineteen fourteen and nineteen fifteen, can finally be brought into action.

These new armies are a remarkable thing. Whole towns have raised whole battalions together. The men of a certain factory, of a certain football club, of a certain office, of a certain street, have signed up side by side, on the promise that they will serve side by side. They are called the Pals battalions. They are eager, well meaning, and largely untested. By the summer of nineteen sixteen, after a year and a half of training, they are ready, or so it is hoped.

For seven days before the attack, more than a million and a half British and French shells fall on the German lines. The noise can be heard in southern England. The plan is for the bombardment to cut every belt of wire and crush every machine gun nest, so that the infantry need only walk forward and occupy the ground. On the still, warm morning of the first of July nineteen sixteen, at seven thirty, whistles blow along the British line, and the men begin to climb out of their trenches.

What happens that morning becomes the great wound of British memory. In many places, the wire has not been cut. In many places, the German machine gun teams, sheltered deep in dugouts cut thirty feet into the chalk, have survived the bombardment. They climb up, set up their guns, and find the British infantry walking toward them in long, even lines, with full kit and rifles slung. By the evening of that day, the British army has suffered some sixty thousand casualties, more than any single day in its history before or since. Twenty thousand of them are dead. Whole Pals battalions, the men of Accrington, of Sheffield, of Leeds, of Newcastle, are cut down in the same fields, often within a few minutes of leaving their trenches.

And yet the offensive does not end. It cannot end. Other corps, on the southern part of the line, have done better, and ground has been gained in the woods of Mametz and the village of Fricourt. Through July and August, the battle continues. There are night attacks on Bazentin Ridge. There is the long, terrible struggle for High Wood and Delville Wood. The names blur together. Each small wood becomes a slow grinding place where men go in and men do not come out.

In the middle of September, the British try something new. Forty-nine strange machines, slow and noisy, climb out of the British lines at dawn near the village of Flers-Courcelette. They look like steel boxes on tracks, with sponsons of small cannon and machine guns on each side. The soldiers call them tanks, the cover name they have been given to disguise their development. Of the forty-nine, only a handful reach the German lines, but those that do break through wire and trenches that no man could break, and the German troops who see them are, for a moment, paralyzed. A British correspondent attached to the army writes, simply, that a new thing has come to the field of war. The machines of nineteen sixteen are crude. Their armor is thin. They overheat. They break down. But the idea is set.

The Battle of the Somme drags on into November, when at last the first heavy snow comes and the staffs allow it to be wound down. The British and French have advanced perhaps six miles in places, less in others. They have suffered some four hundred thousand and two hundred thousand casualties, respectively. The Germans have lost a similar number. In the spring of nineteen seventeen, while the snow is still on the ground, the Germans will quietly withdraw to a new, shorter, better-prepared line a little further east, a system of deep trenches and concrete bunkers they call the Siegfried Stellung, and which the Allies will call the Hindenburg Line. The blood-soaked ground of the Somme will become, almost without a battle, a hollow no-man's-land of abandoned villages.

The new year, nineteen seventeen, opens with a confident French commander named Nivelle, who has replaced Joffre. Nivelle has made his reputation in the recapture of Douaumont, and he is sure he has found a method that will work, a sudden, overwhelming creeping barrage followed by infantry in close order, all timed to the second. He plans a great offensive on the Chemin des Dames, the Ladies' Road, an old ridge of high ground above the river Aisne. In April, after a long, cold spring, his soldiers attack. The Germans are waiting on the high ground in their concrete shelters. Nivelle's perfect plan does not survive contact with the slope. By the second day, his casualties have run far beyond anything he had told his soldiers to expect.

What happens next is something that France has not seen before. In ones and twos, in whole companies, French soldiers begin to refuse to attack. Not to surrender, not to fight the staff, not to abandon the line. They simply will not advance again, not for one more meaningless ridge. They sing the old hymns of the revolution. They send delegates to argue with their officers. The mutinies of nineteen seventeen spread through more than half of the French divisions on the front. The Germans never learn how serious they are, because the French keep them secret with absolute discipline.

Nivelle is removed. Pétain is put back in command. He travels from division to division, listening, eating with the men, promising that there will be no more bloody offensives without proper preparation, that the rotations will improve, that leave will be granted. Some of the ringleaders of the mutinies are tried and shot, but Pétain makes the punishments as few as he can. He tells his staff, simply, that he will wait for the tanks and for the Americans. The French army will hold its line, but it will not bleed itself again as it had at Verdun.

The waiting falls heavily on the British. In Flanders, throughout the summer and autumn of nineteen seventeen, Haig launches a series of attacks aimed at breaking out of the Ypres salient and seizing the Belgian channel ports. Months of artillery preparation churn the low fields into a thick, gripping morass. Then the rains come, the heaviest of any year of the war. The drainage canals are smashed. The shell holes fill with water. The fields become a slow, devouring bog, in which men and horses and guns all sink. The battle is officially named Third Ypres, but the soldiers call it by the name of the ridge they finally take in November, after months of attacks. They call it Passchendaele. After it, the village name will mean, for a generation, the worst that war can do to ground.

In November of that same year, on a cold, clear morning, the British try yet another new thing. At the small town of Cambrai, more than four hundred tanks, supported by cavalry and infantry, attack without any artillery preparation at all, relying on the surprise of the machines to break the wire. They tear a great gap in the Hindenburg Line. Church bells ring in England for the first time since the war began. Then, as so often, reserves are insufficient, the cavalry cannot find a way through, the Germans counterattack with their own newly trained shock troops, and within ten days the gains are largely lost. But again the lesson is being written, in steel and engine oil. The next time, the tanks will go forward in greater numbers, with better tactics, with infantry and aircraft and artillery all woven together.

Through nineteen seventeen, another change is gathering, slowly, on the far side of the Atlantic. Since the spring, the United States has been at war with Germany, drawn in by the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and by a clumsy German telegram that tried to draw Mexico into an alliance against America. The American army of nineteen seventeen is small, only a hundred thousand or so men. Its commander, a stiff, careful general named Pershing, lands in France in June. He is met with crowds, with flowers, with relief. But the bulk of his army is still being raised, being trained, being shipped. It will be a year before the great American Expeditionary Forces can take their place beside the British and the French in any number. For the moment, the men in the trenches must hold on.

The British have prepared the morning of the first of July with great underground works. Tunnels have been driven for weeks beneath certain points of the German line, and packed with explosives. At ten minutes past seven, a few minutes before the infantry climb out, a great mine goes up at Hawthorn Ridge, throwing a column of chalk and earth higher than any building. A few minutes later, a still larger mine fires at Lochnagar, near the village of La Boisselle, leaving behind a crater nearly three hundred feet across, deep enough to swallow a small church. The walls of those craters can still be walked, today, by anyone who finds the right path through the wheat fields above the river Ancre. Larks rise from the grass at the edges of them, just as they did, by the accounts of survivors, on that warm summer morning in nineteen sixteen.

Along the northern sector of the British line, near the village of Beaumont Hamel, the Newfoundland Regiment, made up of fishermen and shopkeepers and farmers from a small dominion across the Atlantic, leaves its trenches at half past nine. The men advance up a long, shallow slope, in plain sight of the German machine guns. Within thirty minutes, more than two thirds of them are dead, dying, or wounded. The morning is still and bright. The hour ends. Almost an entire generation of young men from a particular place, from St. John's and Bonavista and Trinity Bay, has been folded into a single field of barley above the Somme. The first of July is still observed, a hundred years later, in Newfoundland, as a day of remembrance.

The French armies on the southern flank of the offensive do better. Their artillery is denser, their tactics more flexible, their men quietly more experienced from the long bleeding of Verdun. They advance four miles in places, taking villages like Hardecourt and Curlu, taking thousands of prisoners. But the great breakthrough that General Haig had hoped for never comes. Through July and August, the offensive narrows into the long, slow attrition of small woods and ridge lines.

The new tanks at Flers-Courcelette in September, slow and unreliable as they are, are followed by reorganization rather than withdrawal. By the end of nineteen sixteen, a small dedicated tank corps is forming in the rear areas, with its own training grounds and its own doctrine. The senior officers begin to argue about whether the tanks should be used in small batches to support the infantry, or in great massed waves of their own. Both sides of the argument will be tested before the war is out.

While the Somme grinds on, the political shape of the war begins to shift again. In Germany, the failures at Verdun and on the Somme bring down Falkenhayn. He is replaced as chief of the great general staff by the eastern commander Hindenburg, with Ludendorff at his elbow as quartermaster general. The two of them, working in close partnership, will gradually take a power that is greater than the Kaiser's own. In Britain, after a winter of growing public impatience, Asquith is replaced as prime minister by the energetic Lloyd George, who promises to fight the war to the knockout. In France, Joffre too is at last set aside, kicked upstairs to a marshal's baton, and replaced first by Nivelle and then, after his disaster, by Pétain.

In the spring of nineteen seventeen, in the cold green hills of Artois, the four divisions of the Canadian Corps mount a model attack on Vimy Ridge. They have rehearsed for months on a full-scale practice ground laid out behind the lines. Tunnels have been driven beneath the German positions to bring up troops in safety. The artillery uses a tightly timed rolling barrage that the infantry follows step by step. On Easter Monday, the ninth of April, in driving sleet, the Canadians take in three days a ridge that the French had failed to take in two years. Vimy becomes, for the young dominion of Canada, a moment of national arrival. Their soldiers will go on to lead many of the great Allied attacks of the last year of the war.

Further east, in Russia, the strain of the war reaches its breaking point in the same month. The Tsar abdicates in March. A provisional government tries to keep Russia in the war, with one last great offensive in July that ends in collapse. By November, in the streets of Petrograd, Bolshevik soldiers and workers seize the seat of government, and Vladimir Lenin steps from a sealed train into the new role of revolutionary leader. The new government opens negotiations for peace at a place called Brest-Litovsk. By March of nineteen eighteen, after long argument, Russia signs a treaty that takes her out of the war and gives away to Germany an empire of Ukraine, the Baltic provinces, and Poland. For Germany, this is the freeing of fifty divisions of seasoned soldiers for the Western Front. For the Allies, it is the worst news in three years of war.

In Italy, in late October nineteen seventeen, in a thick fog along the river Isonzo, German and Austrian divisions break the Italian line at a small village called Caporetto. The Italian armies fall back nearly seventy miles in confusion, all the way to the river Piave, and most of an Italian army is captured. British and French divisions are rushed south by train across the Alps to stiffen the new line. Caporetto, like Brest-Litovsk, like the slow signs of war weariness in France, is one of the dark hinges of the long year nineteen seventeen.

In the late autumn and winter of nineteen seventeen, the war takes a sharp turn that will shape the final year. To the east, in Russia, two revolutions follow one another. The new Bolshevik government in Petrograd asks for an armistice, and in March nineteen eighteen, in a small fortress town called Brest-Litovsk, Russia signs a separate peace. For Germany, this is a strategic gift. Nearly fifty divisions, hundreds of thousands of soldiers, can be moved by train from the great forests of the east to the muddy fields of the west. For the first time since the autumn of nineteen fourteen, the German army on the Western Front will have a clear local superiority in numbers. The new German first quartermaster, a focused, severe officer named Ludendorff, sees the moment plainly. He must use it before the Americans arrive in strength. He must, as he writes in his diary, finish the war this spring.

He gathers his armies in the gentle country east of the old Somme battlefield. He pulls his best men out of the line and forms them into special assault units, which he calls Stosstruppen, storm troops. They are taught a new way of fighting. They will not advance in long lines. They will move in small, fast groups, infiltrating the enemy line at its weakest points, bypassing strong points, leaving them for the slower troops behind to mop up. They will carry light machine guns, flame throwers, mortars, and grenades, and they will trust in speed.

For the artillery, he turns to a colonel named Bruchmüller, a careful, almost mathematical man, whose plans of fire become so precise that his fellow officers nickname him Durchbruchmüller, breakthrough Müller. He will not pound the enemy positions for days as the British and French have done. He will hammer them all at once, in a hurricane of shells of every kind, gas and high explosive and shrapnel layered in calculated waves, lasting only a few hours. The barrage will smash communications and confuse reserves and isolate the front line. Then the storm troops will go in.

On the morning of the twenty-first of March nineteen eighteen, in a thick spring fog along the old Somme front, sixty four German divisions attack on a line of forty miles. Bruchmüller's barrage falls for five hours. Then the storm troops walk forward through the mist, almost unseen, and slip through gaps in the British line. By the end of the first day, they have torn a hole that has not been seen in three and a half years of fighting. By the end of the first week, the German army has advanced more than thirty miles in places, recapturing all the ground given up in nineteen seventeen, threatening the great rail junction of Amiens. The Allied armies have not been so close to losing the war since the first weeks of nineteen fourteen.

In this crisis, the Allies finally do what they have refused to do for three years. They appoint a single commander to coordinate all their armies on the Western Front. The man chosen is the French general Foch, fierce, cheerful, and stubborn, who is given the title of generalissimo. His method is simple. He sends reserves to the threatened points without regard to which national army holds them. Where Ludendorff's offensive runs out of breath, just short of Amiens, Foch's reserves are quietly assembling.

Operation Michael, the great spring attack, slows in early April. Ludendorff shifts his blow north into Flanders, in an attack he calls Georgette. Once again, German storm troops break the line. Once again, they advance many miles, this time toward the channel ports. The British commander, Haig, issues an order of the day in which he tells his men, simply, that they have their backs to the wall and must fight on to the end. The Germans approach the high ground above Hazebrouck. Then, again, the offensive slows.

In late May, Ludendorff turns south once more, to the old Chemin des Dames, where Nivelle's offensive had failed the year before. His third great attack, Operation Blücher-Yorck, breaks across the Aisne so quickly that within a few days, German troops are back on the river Marne, less than fifty miles from Paris. Long-range guns shell the city itself. The same panic of nineteen fourteen returns. But now, at last, the Americans are arriving. The first division to fight in number is the United States Second Division, including a brigade of marines, who are pushed into a small forest near Belleau, west of the Marne. There, in the heat of June, they fight a slow, fierce battle for a wood barely a mile across, and at the end, they hold it. A few weeks earlier, at a village called Cantigny, the United States First Division has already attacked and held its first prepared position. The American Expeditionary Forces are still small, but they are no longer green.

Ludendorff makes one more attempt, in mid-July, on either side of Reims, in the second battle of the Marne. This time, French and American counterattacks come in on his exposed flank within days. The German advance halts. Then, for the first time since March, it is rolled back. From this moment on, the initiative passes from Germany to the Allies, and it does not return.

On the eighth of August nineteen eighteen, in the early hours before dawn, on the rolling country east of Amiens, the British, French, Australian, and Canadian armies launch what they have learned from four years of failure. Hundreds of tanks, more than six hundred guns per mile of front, and squadrons of low-flying aircraft attack together. There is no preparatory bombardment to warn the Germans, only a sudden, perfectly timed creeping barrage at zero hour. The fog burns away into a clear morning. The German line breaks for eight miles, and the attackers advance up to seven miles in a single day, taking thirty thousand prisoners. Ludendorff will later call this the black day of the German army. He understands, finally, that his men are no longer willing to fight as they once did, that the long retreat home has begun.

The period that follows is called by the Allies the Hundred Days. It is not a single battle, but a long, rolling, coordinated offensive, all along the Western Front, from the channel coast down to the wooded hills of the Argonne. Foch's principle is simple. He attacks at one point, lets the offensive lose its impetus, then strikes at another. The Germans, weary, short of food, short of replacements, must move their reserves from one threatened sector to the next, always too late.

In September, the Americans, at last operating as their own army under Pershing, attack the Saint-Mihiel salient on the southern shoulder of the line. They take it in three days, at light cost, with the help of French armor and a vast Allied air force commanded in part by an American colonel named Mitchell. Within days, Pershing shifts his great force north, into the broken country between the river Meuse and the Argonne forest. There, on the twenty-sixth of September, the Meuse-Argonne offensive opens. It will be the largest battle the United States Army has ever fought, larger than any battle in its history before that day. It will continue, day after day, through dense woods and steep, fortified hills, against the southern pillar of the Hindenburg Line, for forty-seven days, until the war itself ends.

Further north, in late September and early October, the British, Australian, and Canadian forces break the main Hindenburg Line itself, in a series of attacks that involve the canal at Saint-Quentin and the heights of the Beaurevoir Line beyond. They cross the deep trenches and the concrete shelters that the Germans have spent eighteen months building. They go forward, by the end of October, into open country that has not seen war in four years, country with crops still growing in the fields and roofs still whole on the farmhouses.

As the autumn deepens, Germany's allies begin to fall away. In late September, Bulgaria signs an armistice. In late October, the Ottoman Empire follows. In early November, Austria-Hungary asks for terms. In Germany itself, the strain begins to crack the political surface. In late October, sailors of the high seas fleet at Kiel refuse to put to sea for one last, futile sortie. The mutiny spreads to the streets of the port cities. Workers' and soldiers' councils form in Hamburg, in Bremen, in Munich. On the ninth of November, in Berlin, the Kaiser, Wilhelm the Second, abdicates. He boards a train into the neutral Netherlands. A republic is declared in Berlin from a window of the Reichstag.

By then, a small German delegation has crossed the lines under a white flag. They have been received in a railway carriage in a quiet forest clearing near Compiègne, north of Paris. The carriage belongs to the Allied generalissimo, Marshal Foch. The terms presented to them are stern. They include the immediate evacuation of all occupied territory, the surrender of vast quantities of arms and ships, the right of the Allies to occupy the Rhineland. The delegation has no real power to refuse. The new government in Berlin, by telegram, tells them to sign.

In the early hours of the eleventh of November nineteen eighteen, at five o'clock in the morning, the armistice is signed in Foch's railway carriage. By the terms of the agreement, hostilities are to cease at eleven o'clock that same morning, six hours later. Word spreads along the long line in fragments, by telephone, by motorcycle, by runner. In some sectors, men keep firing until the very last moment, sometimes pointlessly, sometimes because they cannot believe it is real. In other places, the guns simply trail off, like a tide going out.

At eleven o'clock, all along the Western Front, the noise stops. Men climb out of their trenches and stand on the parapets, blinking, looking at one another. Birds, which have not been heard in many sectors for years, begin to be audible again in the small woods. Somewhere, a dog barks. A church bell rings, far back, in some town behind the line. The silence that follows is not exactly peace, because the war has gone on for so long that it has become its own weather, but it is the beginning of peace.

In the days that follow, German divisions, in good order, march east, back across the Rhine. Allied divisions begin to move into the Rhineland. The trenches start to be drained, where the rains will let them. Soldiers begin the slow process of going home, to towns and villages all across Europe and across the seas, where lamps are being lit in the windows for them. Some come home soon. Some, the wounded and the prisoners, will come home over months and years. Some will not come home at all, and the long lists of their names will be carved on stone memorials in every town, on village greens, in railway stations, in churches.

This is the story of those four years on the Western Front. The mobilizations of August nineteen fourteen, the long retreat to the Marne, the Race to the Sea, the first Christmas in the trenches. The gas at Ypres, the dogfights above the lines, the Pals battalions on the Somme, the tanks at Flers. Verdun and its sacred road. Passchendaele and its mud. The mutinies of the French army that did not break it. The cold patience of Pétain. The arrival of Pershing's Americans. The hurricane spring of Ludendorff. The black day at Amiens. The hundred days. The carriage in the forest at Compiègne. The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, when a continent, exhausted, fell silent.

Through the long months of that final year, the home fronts of all the warring countries grow tired in their own ways. The Allied blockade has tightened year by year, and in the cities of central Europe, food has become a constant anxiety. Berlin, Vienna, and Budapest live through what the people there will call the turnip winter of nineteen seventeen, when the potato crop fails and turnips, normally fed only to cattle, become the staple of every family meal. Coal is short. Trams stop running. In some neighbourhoods, hospitals close because they cannot heat their wards. By the summer of nineteen eighteen, the cumulative effect of four years of blockade is beginning to be measured in the weights of children and the colour of their skin. None of this is visible to the soldiers in the front line, but they know it is there in the letters from home.

In the spring of nineteen eighteen, almost as a kind of cruel joke layered onto the war, a new strain of influenza begins to move through the camps and the cities. It is unusually severe. It strikes the young as hard as the old. It kills its victims sometimes within a single day, drowning them in their own lungs. It moves with the soldiers as they are sent forward and as they are sent home. By the time the war is over, the so-called Spanish flu will have killed more people, perhaps very many more, than the war itself. In nineteen eighteen, however, no one yet knows how large its shadow will be. It is only one more burden on a world that already has too many.

In the United States, in January nineteen eighteen, President Wilson lays out before Congress a list of fourteen points, simple plain principles for a peace, freedom of the seas, open agreements openly arrived at, an association of nations to maintain peace. The fourteen points will become, in the months ahead, a kind of beacon for the war-weary peoples of central Europe, including the soldiers and civilians of Germany itself. They will read or hear of these terms, and they will believe, with growing hope, that a fair peace is possible if only their governments will sue for it. That hope, more than any single battle, will help to bring down the empires of central Europe in the autumn of the year.

On the Western Front, the Hundred Days roll on. The British and French and Americans and Canadians and Australians and New Zealanders, a vast Allied army built of many nations, push the German line back, week after week. The Germans do not panic. They retreat in good order, fighting rearguard actions in every village and crossroads. Their machine guns, hidden behind hedges and in the upper windows of farmhouses, take a heavy toll on the Allied infantry that follows. But the line keeps moving east. The shapes of villages that none of these soldiers have ever seen before pass them in a slow procession, of red roofs and church spires and apple orchards still bearing fruit in the September sun. The men learn the names of these places only briefly, and then forget them again, because tomorrow there will be another village.

In early October, the German government, under the new chancellor Prince Max of Baden, sends its first note to President Wilson, asking for an armistice on the basis of the fourteen points. Wilson's reply is firm. The terms must come from the Allied military commanders, and Germany must show that it has become a constitutional state. The notes go back and forth across the Atlantic for weeks. While they do, the Allies keep advancing, and the inner fabric of the German Empire keeps cracking. Bavaria declares itself a republic in early November. Austria-Hungary disintegrates into its old national pieces. Czechs and Poles and Hungarians and Slovenes and Croats and Serbs all begin to assemble new countries out of the ruins of an empire that took six centuries to build.

In the early hours of the eleventh of November nineteen eighteen, in the carriage in the forest at Compiègne, the small German delegation, led by a politician named Erzberger, sits at a long polished table across from Marshal Foch, his deputy, an admiral, and their staffs. The terms have been read. Erzberger has tried, with little hope, to soften them. Foch has refused. At a few minutes after five o'clock in the morning, the documents are signed. By the terms agreed there, hostilities are to cease at eleven o'clock that same morning. Foch then withdraws to send the news up the chain to Paris and London and Washington. Erzberger and his colleagues return to their own train, to ride back through the lines under flag of truce. Six hours later, in muddy fields from Switzerland to the sea, the noise of the war stops at last.

In the trenches, men do not always cheer. Some sit down on the firestep and look at their hands, as if they had not seen them in a long time. Some, who have been at the front since nineteen fourteen, simply close their eyes. Some, who have only just arrived, do not understand what has happened. Officers come along the line to tell each company in turn, in clear words, that the armistice is signed and the war is over. Then they step back into their dugouts and sit down with their orderlies and pour out tea.

In the years that follow, the men who have lived through this war will go home, and they will try to begin again. Some will find that they cannot speak of it, and will hold the memory close and silent for the rest of their lives. Some will write, in poems and letters and books that the world is still reading. Some will lay flowers, every November, at the small stone memorials of their towns, where the names of the men who did not return are carved in alphabetical order, and where, year after year, the wreaths are renewed. The fields of the old Western Front, slowly, are returned to grain. Plowmen still turn up shells in the soil, near villages like Vimy and Verdun and Passchendaele, and the great cemeteries of the Commonwealth and of France and of Germany lie quiet beneath their white and grey crosses, in long, patient rows.
